Eshari.lore:
The Eshari are living custodians of death, a sombre people whose senses reach toward the boundary crossed by departing souls. They are neither undead nor creatures of the grave; rather, they regard themselves as wardens of the final passage, protecting the dead from those who would bind, devour or corrupt them.
“The dead rarely trouble the living without reason. Find the reason, and you will find the hand that should concern you.” - Maera Kelvan, Bell-Warden

Eshari civilisation is structured around the concept of the Last Road. They disagree among themselves about what awaits at its end, but most accept that death involves a transition that should occur without coercion. Their sacred responsibility lies at the threshold, not beyond it.
Consequently, Eshari culture is remarkably tolerant of differing beliefs about the afterlife. An Eshari funeral attendant may perform rites for a religion they do not personally follow because the rite exists for the deceased and their family rather than for the attendant. Learning foreign funerary customs is considered a respectable form of scholarship, and experienced Eshari can often identify a culture from its treatment of the dead as readily as another scholar might identify it from language or clothing.
Death is highly visible in Eshari settlements without being oppressive. Memorial walls stand beside markets. Funeral houses occupy central rather than peripheral districts. Children are taught the names of recently deceased neighbours and are encouraged to understand what death means rather than being hidden from it.
Every established community maintains at least one open lantern, traditionally kept burning throughout the night. The practice symbolises that no departing soul should be forced to travel entirely alone. Travellers who die far from home are frequently carried to these lanterns while arrangements are made for whatever rites their own people require.
Service to the dead also extends to protecting the living. Eshari distinguish sharply between a genuinely restless spirit and a corpse being manipulated by something else. Their investigators therefore ask why before reaching for weapons. A haunting created by betrayal may require justice. A soul trapped by necromancy requires release. A predatory entity exploiting grief requires destruction. Simply destroying every manifestation of the dead is regarded as ignorance masquerading as courage.
Soul-binding is among the most serious offences recognised by Eshari culture. Animating empty remains can itself be controversial, but trapping a conscious soul, forcing possession or deliberately preventing the dead from passing onward is regarded far more severely. Those who hunt such practitioners often travel for years following rumours of spirit prisons, stolen remains and fraudulent mediums.
Eshari families do not regard funerary professions as inherently religious. A Bell-Warden might be a devout priest, philosophical sceptic or outright atheist. The Last Road is a cultural understanding of death rather than proof of any specific god.

DESCRIPTION
Eshari are tall, fine-boned humanoids who usually stand between 5½ and 7 feet tall. Their skin ranges from near-white ivory through shades of ash and slate to deep charcoal, often possessing a smooth, muted quality that seems to absorb rather than reflect bright light.
Their eyes are distinctive. The eye itself is dark and glossy, while thin rings of white, pale blue or silver surround the iris. Under low light these rings can appear faintly luminous, giving an Eshari gaze an intensity that has contributed to generations of exaggerated stories about them being able to see souls directly.
Hair is commonly black, grey, silver or colourless and may begin losing pigment comparatively early in life. Many Eshari wear it long during periods of mourning or service and cut it when a major obligation to the dead has been completed, although customs vary considerably between funerary traditions.
The strangest characteristic is their shadow. In dim light an Eshari's shadow occasionally appears to move an instant after they do. The effect is slight—often dismissed by observers as fatigue or flickering illumination—but sufficiently consistent that the Eshari themselves regard it as evidence that some part of them stands fractionally closer to the Veil than other living peoples.
Their clothing tends towards practical ceremonial garments: layered robes, long coats, gloves, veils and easily removable insignia identifying their funerary role. Bells, lanterns and memorial tokens are common accessories, though outsiders often mistake professional tools for religious symbols.
Eshari reach adulthood at around 18 years of age and commonly live for 160 to 200 years. A starting Eshari character has an initial age of 18+2d6 years.
Eshari.mechanics:
Ability Modifiers Con +1, Wis +1, Cha +1, Str -1; Size: Medium; Speed: 25 feet; Power Points: 0
LANGUAGES
Core Languages: Low Tongue, Vesperic; Additional Languages: Choose from any common or regional language.
SPECIALIST SKILLS
You gain Eshari Lore and Spirit Lore as specialist skills.
OTHER ABILITIES
Nightvision: You can see in dark areas and, with a small amount of light, can see well.
Soul Warden: You gain a +1 racial bonus to saving throws against Soul Drain, possession and effects with the Soul trait.
Spirit Sense: You possess Spirit Sense as a tertiary sense. When you use Search (Perception), you can detect the presence and general direction of disembodied spirits, incorporeal undead, haunts and active possession within 30 feet. You cannot determine exact location, identity or allegiance through this sense alone. Spirit Sense is blocked by 1 foot of stone, 1 inch of common metal or any thickness of lead.

Kethrani.lore:
The Kethrani are living testaments, a people born with lines of sacred script embedded within their skin. New symbols appear throughout their lives without ink, blade or conscious choice, recording concepts that priests have spent centuries attempting to interpret.
“The gods did not write upon me so that priests might agree.” - Oran Serel, Speaker of the Unfinished Verse

Kethrani society has developed around an uncomfortable reality: everyone else wants their bodies to mean something.
From birth, Kethrani are studied by priests, theologians, prophets, linguists and occasionally rulers. Consequently, one of the strongest principles in Kethrani culture is bodily and interpretative autonomy. The Testament may be sacred, but the person bearing it is not public property.
Most communities maintain Houses of Interpretation, institutions combining libraries, schools, meeting halls and places of worship. Kethrani families voluntarily record new passages appearing upon their bodies, allowing scholars to compare recurring symbols across generations. Detailed sketches, rubbings and written transcriptions are maintained, but permission is considered essential. Secretly copying another Kethrani's Testament is treated as a profound violation of trust.
The Testament does not provide simple commandments. Passages contradict one another, change context when new lines appear and frequently resemble fragments taken from theological traditions that historically opposed each other. This has prevented any single unified Kethrani religion from emerging.
Instead, Kethrani philosophy emphasises interpretation without surrendering choice. A sacred message can offer wisdom, warning or responsibility, but it cannot relieve the recipient of moral agency. The old proverb that “revelation without choice is merely another chain” is taught to children almost as soon as they begin asking what their own markings mean.
Dominant Verses shape social roles without functioning as rigid castes. A child whose Testament repeatedly emphasises Mercy may be encouraged towards healing, but nobody is required to become what their skin appears to describe. Indeed, choosing a radically different life is sometimes interpreted as part of the Testament's meaning.
Changes in the script frequently accompany spiritual crises, moments of great personal decision or exposure to powerful divine phenomena. New passages may emerge overnight after a near-death experience, remain incomprehensible for decades and suddenly acquire meaning after the bearer meets a particular person or visits an unfamiliar place.
This has made Kethrani adventurers common. Some pursue an apparent prophecy. Others seek scholars capable of translating a newly appeared passage. Many simply leave because they are tired of living among people who read their arms before looking at their faces.

DESCRIPTION
Kethrani possess the same broad range of builds, complexions, hair colours and facial features found among humans. What immediately distinguishes them is the Testament—the sacred script that develops naturally beneath their skin.
The first marks normally appear around the heart, brow, hands or along the centre of the chest. During childhood they may resemble isolated glyphs, but as a Kethrani matures the marks spread into lines, circles, repeated invocations, diagrams and dense blocks of writing. Some Testaments remain relatively sparse while others eventually cover most of the body.
Colour varies enormously. Some marks appear black as fresh ink, others white as scar tissue, bronze, silver or gold. Certain passages shine faintly when exposed to darkness or intensify during prayer, danger or emotional stress. No reliable relationship exists between colour and meaning.
The script lies beneath the skin rather than upon it. Tattooing over a Testament may obscure it temporarily, but the original marks gradually become visible again. Injury behaves more strangely. If a section of skin bearing the Testament is badly scarred, portions of the script may appear fragmented during healing before slowly reforming around the scar. This has led some theologians to argue that the Testament belongs to the Kethrani's soul rather than their body.
Clothing varies according to personal attitude. Some Kethrani deliberately expose large portions of their Testament as an expression of identity. Others wear high collars, gloves and layered garments because they resent being stared at, interpreted or treated as religious objects. This choice can itself be politically charged in communities where Kethrani scripture is considered holy.
Kethrani reach physical adulthood at around 16 years of age and usually live between 120 and 160 years. New markings continue to appear throughout life, often accelerating during periods of spiritual crisis. A starting Kethrani character has an initial age of 16+2d6 years.
Kethrani.mechanics:
Ability Modifiers Int +1, Wis +1, Cha +1, Dex -1; Size: Medium; Speed: 25 feet; Power Points: 0
LANGUAGES
Core Languages: High Tongue, Low Tongue; Additional Languages: Choose from any common or regional language.
SPECIALIST SKILLS
You gain Kethrani Lore and Theology as specialist skills.
OTHER ABILITIES
Living Testament: You gain a +1 racial bonus to Religion and Linguistics checks made to identify, translate or understand prayers, religious symbols, divine doctrine and sacred writings.
Revelatory Script: You gain Read Aura as a divinity innate cantrip with the Focus trait.
Sacred Inscription: The Testament is difficult to overwrite with hostile spiritual authority. You gain a +1 racial bonus to saving throws against curse effects.

Myrathi.lore:
The Myrathi are fungal humanoids linked to vast ancestral mycelia beneath the earth. When one of their people dies, the body is not entombed or burned but planted, allowing memory and personality to seep into a living network known as the Ancestral Bloom.
“We bury no wisdom. We plant it.” - Thren Vaelori, Speaker Beneath the Roots

A Myrathi settlement is built as much below ground as above it. The centre of Myrathi civilisation is the Ancestral Bloom. A mature settlement is less a collection of buildings than a living organism spread across and beneath the surrounding land. Homes, halls and gardens exist above ground, but below them stretches the mycelial network containing centuries of accumulated memory.
The dead are planted rather than buried. The body is placed into prepared soil and joined to the Bloom. Decomposition is not hidden or regarded as desecration; it is the final act through which the deceased returns nourishment and experience to the community.
This practice produces significant misunderstanding with other cultures. Myrathi can find embalming deeply strange, interpreting the deliberate prevention of decomposition as refusing to allow the dead to finish giving themselves back to the world. Most nevertheless respect foreign funerary customs and understand that handling another people's dead without permission is a serious offence.
What enters the Bloom is not a fully conscious person. Memories fragment. Skills become impressions. Emotional associations persist long after names have disappeared. One ancestor may remember the smell of a particular poison but not who used it; another may preserve decades of agricultural knowledge while every personal relationship has faded.
Consequently, ancestral communion is rarely simple. Myrathi sayings describe the Bloom as a room filled with a thousand elderly relatives trying to answer the same question at once. Wisdom lies in recognising which memory matters.
This has also prevented the development of absolute ancestor worship. The dead were people, and people could be mistaken. A recurring Myrathi principle states that memory deserves attention, not obedience.
Myrathi kinship is strongly connected to the Bloom in which someone was raised. Biological parentage matters but belonging to the same ancestral network can be equally significant. Individuals adopted into another settlement may eventually contribute so much experience that future generations regard them as inseparable from that Bloom's ancestry.
Travellers therefore perform an important cultural function. A Myrathi adventurer is not necessarily leaving their community behind; they may be extending its experience. Returning travellers spend long periods describing what they have seen, meditating in contact with the mycelium and deliberately committing memories to the network.
Destroyed Blooms are among the greatest tragedies imaginable to Myrathi. Survivors sometimes preserve a fragment of living mycelium and carry it for years in specially prepared containers, searching for suitable ground where the ancestral network can be established again.

DESCRIPTION
Myrathi are upright fungal humanoids standing between 4½ and 6½ feet tall. Myrathi are unmistakably non-human. Their bodies are formed from dense fibrous flesh arranged around a flexible internal lattice rather than conventional bone. Their silhouettes nevertheless remain broadly humanoid: two arms, two legs, a head and an upright stance, although individuals vary far more dramatically than most flesh-and-blood peoples.
Colour ranges from pale cream, ivory and ochre through rust-red, violet, indigo and near-black. Some possess relatively smooth surfaces resembling thick mushroom stems, while others develop bark-like plates, layered gills or overlapping fungal ridges.
The head is particularly variable. Many Myrathi possess broad cap-like crests, sometimes close to the skull and sometimes extending dramatically beyond it. Others develop fan-shaped structures, layered shelves or crowns of smaller growths. Fine sensory filaments may hang from the scalp, chin or shoulders and can resemble hair when viewed from a distance.
Bioluminescence is common but not universal. Small points of blue, green, violet, amber or white light may form beneath the skin, around gills or along the edges of a cap. These lights can subtly change in brightness according to physical condition and emotional state, though interpretation requires familiarity with the individual.
Myrathi clothing is designed around bodies that may continue changing shape during adulthood. Wrapped cloth, cords, belts and layered panels are preferred over rigid tailoring. Armour produced by Myrathi craftspeople often incorporates natural gaps for caps, gills and sensory growths. Wood, woven fungus, hardened fibre, polished shell and cultivated leather-like materials are common decorative elements.
To outsiders, Myrathi frequently smell faintly of earth, rain, leaves or mushrooms. Individual colonies develop distinctive scents due to the fungi cultivated around their settlements, allowing experienced Myrathi travellers to identify someone's home Bloom before hearing their accent.
Myrathi mature rapidly, reaching adulthood at around 12 years of age, and usually live between 90 and 120 years. An individual body is mortal, but its memories may persist in an Ancestral Bloom for centuries. A starting Myrathi character has an initial age of 11+1d8 years.
Myrathi.mechanics:
Ability Modifiers Con +1, Int +1, Wis +1, Dex -1; Size: Medium; Speed: 25 feet; Power Points: 0
LANGUAGES
Core Languages: Low Tongue, Mycelic; Additional Languages: Choose from any common or regional language.
SPECIALIST SKILLS
You gain Myrathi Lore and Ancestor Lore as specialist skills.
OTHER ABILITIES
Fungal Physiology: You gain a +2 racial bonus to saving throws against disease and poison.
ANCESTRAL COMMUNION
CONCENTRATE FOCUS
Action 1 AP
You quiet your own thoughts and allow inherited fragments of memory to surface. The next Recall Knowledge check you attempt before the end of your next turn gains advantage.
Ancestral Communion does not allow you to attempt a check that would otherwise be impossible, nor does it grant knowledge that could never have been possessed by the Myrathi or their ancestors.

Rhevani.lore:
The Rhevani are a people of returning souls, mortals whose lives are threaded through centuries of death and rebirth. Every Rhevani carries within them fragments of earlier incarnations: a half-remembered face, an instinctive movement, a forgotten prayer or the certainty that they have stood in a place they have never visited. “I do not fear that I will die. I fear only which parts of me the next life will remember.” - Serai Velan, Keeper of the Seventh Memory

The central tension within Rhevani culture is the relationship between continuity and individuality. Reincarnation is accepted as fact, but the returning soul is not considered the same thing as the returning person. A child who remembers being a soldier three centuries ago is still a child. They do not inherit that soldier's authority, marriage, profession or possessions merely because fragments of the old life remain within them.
This distinction lies at the heart of Rhevani law. Property ordinarily passes through conventional living inheritance, while obligations connected directly to the soul are considered individually. An ancient vow might survive reincarnation if the returning Rhevani willingly acknowledges it, but few communities permit creditors to pursue a child for debts incurred by a previous incarnation. The question becomes much more difficult when sacred obligations, unfinished guardianships or magically binding promises are involved.
Most settlements maintain a Hall of Memory, containing ledgers recording births, deaths, unusual childhood recollections, distinctive marks, significant vows and the dying words of those who consented to have them preserved. These records are not merely genealogical. They are tools used during the Rite of Remembering, when elders compare emerging memories with preserved accounts of the dead. Skilled investigators deliberately seek contradictions as readily as similarities, since false identification of a returning soul can damage several families at once.
Rhevani children are encouraged to describe spontaneous memories but discouraged from being coached. Asking a child repeatedly whether they remember a particular person is considered deeply irresponsible. Wealthy families have occasionally attempted to manufacture evidence that a prestigious ancestor has returned among them, and several infamous historical disputes began when rival houses claimed the same child as the reincarnation of an important figure.
Death itself is consequently treated with sadness but little fear. Funerals concentrate less upon promises of reunion and more upon release. The deceased is remembered, their current life is formally declared complete, and the community expresses the hope that whatever returns will be allowed to become something new. Attempts to preserve a soul indefinitely within a corpse, gem, phylactery or similar vessel are especially abhorrent to many Rhevani, who consider such practices the theft of every future life that soul might otherwise have lived.
Rhevani relationships with organised religion vary widely. Some see reincarnation as evidence of a greater divine design, while others regard it as a natural property of souls requiring no deity at all. Ancestor worship is uncommon in its strictest sense because the ancestor may already be alive again somewhere else. Instead, Rhevani tend to honour lives rather than permanently distinct ancestral spirits.

Adventurers occupy an important place within Rhevani culture. Travelling allows unresolved memories to be tested against real places and historical evidence. Some leave home because they repeatedly dream of a ruined tower, forgotten battlefield or unknown face. Others deliberately flee communities obsessed with identifying their previous incarnation. For many Rhevani, adventure is ultimately an attempt to answer a deceptively difficult question: what belongs to my soul, and what belongs only to me?
DESCRIPTION
Rhevani resemble humans in broad form, standing between 5 and 6½ feet tall and weighing between 110 and 220 pounds. Rhevani resemble humans closely enough that at a distance they are often mistaken for them. They possess the same broad variation in complexion, build, facial structure and hair colour, although generations of intermarriage within Rhevani communities have produced certain features that outsiders sometimes describe as unusually symmetrical or strangely familiar. It is not uncommon for someone meeting a Rhevani for the first time to experience the uncomfortable sensation that they have seen that face before.
The eyes provide the clearest indication of Rhevani ancestry. Rather than a single band of colour, a Rhevani iris contains two or more concentric rings, sometimes of subtly different shades and sometimes of dramatically contrasting colours. Gold may surround blue, grey may break into green, or several increasingly pale rings may radiate from the pupil. Rhevani poets describe these as the circles of the returning soul, although scholars have never established any relationship between the number of rings and the number of previous incarnations.
Many Rhevani also possess echo-scars, pale birthmarks resembling wounds, burns, brands or ritual incisions. These marks are present from birth and do not normally cause pain. In rare cases, an echo-scar corresponds closely to the recorded death of an earlier incarnation. Such discoveries are treated seriously but cautiously; Rhevani communities have learned through painful experience that resemblance alone is not proof of spiritual continuity.
Dress varies considerably between communities, but Rhevani commonly incorporate objects associated with memory into their clothing. Small portrait medallions, copied signatures, fragments of old letters and tokens inherited from identified past lives may be worn beside possessions belonging entirely to the current incarnation. This mixture is deliberate. A Rhevani is expected to acknowledge who they might once have been without allowing the dead to consume the person they are now.
Rhevani reach physical adulthood at around 20 years of age and normally live between 110 and 150 years. The soul may return many times, but each incarnation possesses an entirely new body. A starting Rhevani character has an initial age of 19+2d6 years.
Rhevani.mechanics:
Ability Modifiers Int +1, Wis +1, Cha +1, Con -1; Size: Medium; Speed: 25 feet; Power Points: 0
LANGUAGES
Core Languages: Low Tongue, Rhevic; Additional Languages: Choose from any common or regional language.
SPECIALIST SKILLS
You gain Rhevani Lore and Soul Lore as specialist skills.
OTHER ABILITIES
Continuity of Self: You gain a +1 racial bonus to saving throws against possession and mental effects that alter, erase or suppress your memories or identity.
PAST-LIFE ECHO
CONCENTRATE FOCUS
Action 1 AP
You allow a fragment of experience from an earlier incarnation to rise into conscious memory. Select one non-specialist skill. Until the end of your next turn, you gain a +2 racial bonus to checks made using that skill and may use actions that normally require at least 1 rank in that skill as though you possessed 1 rank.
This ability does not grant access to specialist skills, feats or other options with separate prerequisites.

heritages.Ashen:
Ashen Eshari oversee cremation, purification and situations in which remains cannot safely be preserved. They are traditionally called upon after plague, supernatural contamination or encounters with dangerous Undead where ordinary burial would risk further harm.
Generations of association with flame have produced distinctive cultural traditions around fire. Ashen funeral houses are warm, heavily ventilated places scented with smoke, cedar and bitter herbs. Many Ashen carry permanent traces of this environment with them: warm skin, faint smoky scents and robes designed to shed ash easily. They tend to be practical about destruction, regarding fire not as an expression of wrath but as the final means of ensuring that something dangerous can harm nobody again.
You gain resistance to fire and are immune to the harmful effects of mundane smoke produced by ordinary fires.
heritages.Kelvan:
Kelvan are the bell-keepers. Their tradition teaches that sound carries meaning across the Veil more cleanly than sight, and ritual bells accompany funerals, exorcisms, grave vigils and the investigation of restless dead.
Kelvan bells are intensely personal objects. Some are inherited through families while others are forged for a specific individual and buried with them. Different tones may indicate warning, mourning, safe passage or challenge. A trained Kelvan can often recognise another community's funerary practice merely from its bells. Their Sacred Toll represents the most direct expression of a tradition founded upon the belief that even the dead can sometimes be reminded that their mortal time has ended.
You gain Sacred Toll.
SACRED TOLL
AUDITORY DIVINITY FOCUS
Action 1 AP; Range 30 feet; Target one Undead or Unliving creature that can hear you
The target attempts a level-based Will saving throw.
Heroic/Critical The target is unaffected.
Success The target is unaffected.
Partial The target becomes frightened 1 until the end of its next turn.
Failure The target becomes frightened 2 until the end of its next turn.
Fumble The target becomes frightened 2 and cannot use reactions until the end of its next turn.
Blunder The target becomes frightened 3 and cannot use reactions until the end of its next turn.
heritages.Lumari:
Lumari are lantern-bearers, escorts and comforters of the dying. Their softly luminous bodies have made them enduring symbols of the Last Road, and many Eshari communities choose Lumari to accompany funeral processions after sunset.
Their role extends far beyond ceremony. Lumari frequently become guides, hospice workers and travellers who seek those likely to die far from home. The light they carry is traditionally regarded not as something that drives darkness away, but as a promise that somebody remains present within it. Many Lumari therefore cultivate calm, patient personalities, remaining beside the frightened or dying long after others have found excuses to leave.
You emit dim light within 10 feet and can suppress or restore this light as a 1 AP action with the Concentrate trait. Furthermore, you gain Guidance as a divinity innate cantrip with the Focus trait.
heritages.Velari:
Velari devote themselves to watching the Veil. They train from childhood to recognise subtle disturbances, unusual behaviour and the tiny inconsistencies that may betray possession.
This can make Velari unnerving companions. They notice pauses in conversation, glance towards empty corners and sometimes interrupt ordinary activity to investigate something nobody else perceived. Among the Eshari these behaviours are signs of professional attention rather than eccentricity. Velari make excellent haunt investigators, exorcists and guardians of places where spiritual boundaries have become dangerously thin.
The range of your Spirit Sense increases to 60 feet, and you gain a +1 racial bonus to Perception checks made to locate spirits, haunts, possession and undead creatures.
heritages.Morrin:
Morrin are the body-keepers and tomb-wardens of Eshari society. Broader and more powerfully built than many of their kin, they traditionally perform the labour associated with preparing graves, moving remains, guarding reliquaries and defending burial grounds.
Their reputation for physical strength sometimes obscures the delicacy of their work. Morrin are often expert embalmers, restorers of damaged remains and custodians of fragile memorial objects. Their funerary philosophy emphasises stewardship: a body may no longer house its owner, but it remains important to those left behind and should not be treated carelessly.
You gain an additional +1 racial bonus to Constitution.
heritages.Avenor:
Avenor Testaments favour open hands, broken chains, shelters, vessels and repeated phrases associated with preservation and relief. The script is often concentrated around the palms, forearms and heart.
Avenor are traditionally associated with healing, diplomacy and sanctuary. Many feel a strong emotional response to suffering even when they possess no formal medical training. Their communities often remind them that mercy does not require endless self-sacrifice; one of the most common dangers facing young Avenor is allowing other people to turn compassion into obligation.
You gain a +1 racial bonus to Medicine checks and gain Stabilize as a divinity innate cantrip with the Focus trait.
heritages.Korath:
Korath markings form balanced lines, divided circles, watchful eyes and dense statements concerning actions and consequence. Their Testaments often become visibly more pronounced when witnessing a serious dispute.
Korath are frequently drawn towards law, investigation and positions of responsibility, though their concept of judgement is broader than punishment. The most respected Korath are known for patience and insistence upon evidence. The least respected decide that having the Verse of Judgement makes every personal opinion a divine verdict. Kethrani culture regards that mistake as both dangerous and embarrassingly common.
You gain a +1 racial bonus to Intimidate and Sense Motive checks. When you successfully Demoralise a creature, its frightened condition cannot be reduced below 1 until the end of your next turn.
heritages.Sapiren:
Sapiren Testaments contain names, diagrams, nested questions and passages whose grammar resembles lists of observations rather than conventional scripture. Their markings often cluster around the brow, eyes and hands.

Sapiren tend to be curious, analytical and dissatisfied with unsupported certainty. Many accumulate specialist interests with remarkable intensity, surrounding themselves with notes, specimens and unfinished investigations. They have a reputation for answering a simple question with three better questions, a habit other Kethrani find either admirable or exhausting.
You gain an additional +1 racial bonus to Intelligence and may select any one Lore specialist skill.
heritages.Serel:
Serel script frequently forms mirrored phrases, repeated statements and symbols that alter subtly depending upon the angle from which they are viewed. Some passages grow brighter in the presence of deliberate deception, though they are not infallible lie detectors.
Serel are often associated with witnesses, mediators and investigators. Their tradition places enormous importance upon the difference between truth and certainty. A person can speak honestly and still be wrong. Serel children are taught early that exposing deception does not automatically grant understanding of what actually happened.
You gain advantage on saving throws against illusion effects and a +1 racial bonus to Detect Deception (Sense Motive) checks.
heritages.Tharos:
Tharos Testaments form walls, nested circles, interlocking lines and script wrapping protectively around joints, hearts and vital organs. When their innate protective power manifests, these patterns briefly flare with light.
Tharos commonly become guards, carers and defenders, but the Verse is interpreted as protection rather than aggression. The oldest Tharos teaching warns that a shield can become a cage if the person behind it is never permitted to choose their own danger. Consequently, mature Tharos place considerable importance upon distinguishing protection from control.
You gain Warding Word.
WARDING WORD
DIVINITY FOCUS WARDING
Action R
Trigger You or an ally within 10 feet is targeted by an attack
The protective script upon your body flashes with sudden light. The target of the triggering attack gains a +1-status bonus to DB against that attack.
heritages.Karuum:
Karuum (sometimes called Ironcap) develop dense fibrous tissue and overlapping plates across the shoulders, chest and limbs. Their caps are commonly thick, ridged and comparatively compact, giving them a heavy, durable appearance.
They traditionally work in construction, excavation and defence, particularly within the deepest portions of a settlement where collapse or hostile underground creatures pose constant threats. Karuum culture values reliability more than aggression. An Ironcap who promises to hold a tunnel, carry a burden or protect a chamber is expected to remain there long after more flamboyant companions have discovered somewhere else to be heroic.
Your hardened body grants you Base DR 1.
heritages.Lumeri:
Lumeri possess clusters of bioluminescent nodules, luminous gills or softly glowing growths across the head, shoulders and upper body. Their light ranges from warm amber and pale green to cold blue or violet.
Traditionally they guide travellers through underground settlements and tend paths linking distant sections of a Bloom. Their association with illumination has also made them common spirit-speakers and ritual attendants. Myrathi symbolism treats their light as memory itself: something passed from one being to another without being diminished by sharing.
You emit dim light within 10 feet and can suppress or restore this light as a 1 AP action with the Concentrate trait. Furthermore, you gain Guidance as a verdant innate cantrip with the Focus trait.
heritages.Morrai:
Morrai develop most strongly in old burial groves, ancestral chambers and places saturated with generations of decomposition and spiritual memory. Their colouring is often subdued—black, grey, deep violet or bone-white—and some possess cap patterns resembling rings, eyes or branching veins.
Other creatures sometimes assume Morrai are sinister, an interpretation the Myrathi find peculiar. Gravecaps are associated not with death as horror but with the point at which physical decay and ancestral memory meet. They frequently become guardians of planting grounds, spirit mediators and specialists in phenomena that threaten the integrity of the soul.
You gain resistance to essence damage.
heritages.Nethri:
Nethri possess exceptionally fine sensory filaments along the head, neck and limbs. These structures constantly exchange minute chemical and spiritual signals with surrounding Myrathi, creating a subtle level of communication outsiders rarely notice.
Nethri gatherings can therefore appear unnaturally quiet. Entire conversations may take place through tiny changes of posture, scent and transmitted impressions before a spoken word becomes necessary. This does not make Nethri a hive mind—individual thought remains entirely distinct—but it does give them a reputation for emotional sensitivity and an ability to recognise tension within a group before anybody openly acknowledges it.
You gain a +1 racial bonus to Sense Motive checks. In addition, you can communicate silently with willing Myrathi within 60 feet, provided you share a language and neither of you is completely sealed away from the surrounding air.
heritages.Vaelori:
Vaelori produce specialised spores that assist decomposition, suppress harmful rot and support the health of cultivated fungal networks. They are therefore gardeners, healers and corpse-tenders in equal measure, occupations that Myrathi culture sees as closely related.
A Vaelori may spend the morning treating a sick child, the afternoon pruning diseased fungal growth and the evening preparing a body for planting. All three acts are understood as maintaining the health of the same living cycle. Their familiarity with decay can make outsiders uncomfortable, but Vaelori rarely see a contradiction between reverence for life and acceptance of decomposition. To them, one makes the other possible.

You gain a +1 racial bonus to Medicine checks and gain Purify as a verdant innate spell with the Focus trait.
heritages.Arathi:
Arathi souls return most strongly to lives shaped by conflict. Their echoes are not necessarily memories of great warriors; they may come from hunters, guards, caravan defenders, rebels or ordinary people who survived violent times. What persists is physical instinct. An Arathi may catch a falling weapon with a movement they were never taught, instinctively choose defensible ground or awaken from sleep already reaching for an absent sword.
Arathi culture does not assume that such individuals must become soldiers. Indeed, some consciously reject martial professions because they are tired of lives defined by violence. Even these Arathi tend to possess a visible alertness: weight balanced naturally, attention drawn towards entrances and an uncanny tendency to react before others have recognised danger.
You gain an additional +1 racial bonus to Strength and a +10 racial bonus to Initiative checks.
heritages.Dornai:
Dornai carry echoes of people who endured. Many past incarnations appear to have been guardians, rescuers, labourers, survivors and individuals who refused death long enough to complete some essential task. Dornai often describe moments of crisis as strangely familiar, accompanied by the certainty that they have been more exhausted, more wounded or more frightened before—and continued regardless.
Among Rhevani, Dornai are strongly associated with unfinished responsibilities. Families sometimes watch them carefully for signs of inherited vows, though wise elders discourage turning every stubborn child into the reincarnation of some legendary protector. Dornai themselves frequently develop a strong dislike of leaving work incomplete and are disproportionately represented among bodyguards, healers, rescuers and those who remain behind when others retreat. Your Death State increases by 2.
heritages.Sevrai:
Sevrai souls remember movement. Roads, coastlines, mountain passes and the internal geometry of unfamiliar cities sometimes feel more familiar to them than people do. They often acquire languages quickly, imitate foreign customs with ease and experience flashes of recognition when arriving somewhere they have never consciously visited.
Many Sevrai become messengers, merchants, guides, explorers or pilgrims, but the defining characteristic is not wanderlust alone. A Sevrai may settle permanently while still surrounding themselves with maps and travellers' stories. Others feel a persistent restlessness when they remain in one place too long, as though several former lives are quietly reminding them that somewhere beyond the horizon is a road they once failed to finish.
Your land Speed increases by 5 feet, and you learn one additional common or regional language.
heritages.Thaeli:
Thaeli carry echoes associated with prayer, contemplation and spiritual practice. They may instinctively know the rhythm of a liturgy they have never heard, adopt an unfamiliar meditative posture or recognise the emotional weight of a sacred place without understanding its doctrine.
These memories do not necessarily draw a Thaeli towards the same religion followed in a previous incarnation. Rhevani theology strongly warns against assuming that spiritual familiarity equals divine command. A Thaeli may remember kneeling before an altar while profoundly disagreeing with everything that altar now represents. Their heritage is therefore associated as much with spiritual sensitivity as with conventional piety.
You gain Guidance as a divinity innate cantrip with the Focus trait.
heritages.Velori:
Velori are haunted by learning. Their dreams contain classrooms whose walls have long collapsed, arguments with forgotten teachers and books that no surviving library possesses. A Velori may find an obsolete tool strangely intuitive or experience frustration when confronted with a problem they possess the emotional certainty of once knowing how to solve.
This often produces relentless scholars. Velori are strongly represented among Archivists, Folkwarden, historians and investigators, particularly those searching for lost knowledge. Others find the experience deeply frustrating: remembering that an answer once existed is not the same as remembering the answer itself. For such Velori, every recovered fragment of forgotten knowledge feels less like discovery and more like finally completing a sentence interrupted by death.
You gain an additional +1 racial bonus to Intelligence and may select any one Lore specialist skill appropriate to a former life.

Battlefield Chaplain.description: You carried faith into places where sermons were drowned by steel. Whether attached to a formal army, a mercenary company or a desperate militia, you tended the frightened, witnessed final words and reminded exhausted soldiers why they still stood. You may have left military service behind, but you remain accustomed to offering calm when everyone around you expects to die.

Doctrine Keeper.description: You were entrusted with preserving the teachings of a faith: copying approved texts, comparing interpretations and learning which words carried authority within your order. You know that doctrine is rarely as simple as outsiders believe, and that a single disputed line can divide temples, dynasties or nations. Adventure now gives you the chance to test what you learned against a much larger world.

Excommunicate.description: Once you belonged to a recognised faith, but that relationship ended badly. Perhaps you challenged a superior, broke a sacred rule, uncovered corruption or simply refused to recant a belief. You still understand the language, customs and weaknesses of organised religion, even if its doors are now closed to you. Whether you seek reconciliation, vindication or freedom is entirely your own affair.

Funeral Cantor.description: You learned the songs, prayers and spoken rites used to honour the dead. Your work took you into homes at their most vulnerable, onto battlefields after the fighting ended and into burial grounds where the living wanted reassurance that the deceased had been treated correctly. You understand that mourning has rules, but also that every culture sings its grief differently.

Grave Custodian.description: Cemeteries, crypts and ossuaries were once your workplace. You maintained graves, repaired seals, recorded interments and watched for signs that the dead had been disturbed. Most nights were quiet. The nights that were not taught you why burial customs, wards and careful records matter. You have since left the graveyard behind, though you remain difficult to surprise among the dead.

Oath Witness.description: You served as a recognised witness to vows, contracts, reconciliations and sacred promises. Your presence did not make an oath magical, but it made the words difficult to deny later. Years spent observing nervous petitioners, ambitious nobles and desperate families taught you to hear hesitation and recognise when someone is shaping a promise to leave themselves an escape.

Pilgrim Envoy.description: Your journeys began as acts of devotion, carrying you from shrine to shrine and through communities whose customs differed sharply from your own. Along the road you became as much messenger as pilgrim, carrying letters, settling small disputes and explaining one faith to another. You are comfortable travelling with little and speaking respectfully even when you do not share another person's beliefs.

Reliquary Seeker.description: You devoted yourself to finding sacred objects that had been lost, stolen or forgotten. Some relics were genuine, others were elaborate frauds, and more than one proved dangerous to everyone who tried to possess it. Your experience taught you to examine provenance, symbolism and the stories surrounding an object before accepting claims of holiness at face value.

Sacred Chirurgeon.description: You trained in a religious infirmary where prayer accompanied practical medicine rather than replacing it. You learned to cut, stitch, splint and cleanse while priests dealt with matters of soul and spirit. Your hands are steady around blood and pain, and you have seen enough suffering to know that faith is most useful when accompanied by competent treatment.

Shrine Mason.description: You helped build and maintain places of worship: roadside shrines, burial chapels, temple walls, sacred wells or monumental sanctuaries. Your craft taught you which symbols must face the sunrise, how old foundations conceal earlier holy sites and why priests become extremely particular about the placement of doors. You now carry those practical skills into ruins and forgotten sacred places.

Spirit Medium.description: Since childhood you have been unusually receptive to presences that others overlook. Training taught you to distinguish genuine spirits from grief, deception and imagination, and to approach the unseen with caution rather than blind obedience. Some mediums work in temples, others serve villages or families, while a few wander because too many voices know where they live.

Temple Chronicler.description: You spent years recording the life of a religious institution: births, deaths, appointments, miracles, disputes, donations, pilgrimages and scandals carefully omitted from the public sermons. Archives taught you that faith leaves a paper trail, and that old records often reveal truths the living would prefer forgotten. Adventuring offers access to histories that no orderly archive could ever contain.
